compare.br: In Brazil, “feijão com arroz” is an everyday meal, and people often ask the cook, “Tem carne?” before they eat.
compare.us: In the USA, many people say clearly what they can’t eat: I’m vegan, I’m allergic to nuts, I don’t eat pork.
compare.tip: Use “I don’t eat…” for a rule and “I’m allergic to…” for health.

pages.title: The dumpling stand · 1/3
paragraphs: Mei has a small dumpling stand in **San Francisco**. Every day, people come and say, “**Yum!** These smell good.” Mei smiles. “**Try one**,” she says.

One day, a woman called Nina comes to the stand. “**What’s in it?**” she asks. “Pork and cabbage,” says Mei. “**I don’t eat pork**,” says Nina. “**Do you have** chicken?” “Yes! Chicken and mushroom,” says Mei.
pages.prompt: Onde começa e o que acontece?

pages.title: The dumpling stand · 2/3
paragraphs: Nina eats one. “**Perfect!** How much?” “**Six for eight dollars**,” says Mei. Nina buys six, and she tries the sauce. It is a little spicy. “**It’s fire!**” she laughs, and drinks some water.

Mei thinks about her grandmother’s story. It is a fairy tale from Germany, “Hansel and Gretel”. The Brothers Grimm collected it in 1812. Two children find a house of bread, cake and candy. “Are these sweet?” they ask. Mei’s dumplings are not sweet, but the children in her street love them too.

pages.title: The dumpling stand · 3/3
paragraphs: Nina comes back the next week. “**Enjoy the dumplings!**” says Mei. Now Nina is a happy customer, and she tells her friends about the little stand.
